label: Outside witness
knownFor: A Jewish priest and historian at Rome, whose Jewish Antiquities names Jesus and his brother James.
datesNote: Born 37; the year of his death is not recorded

keyWorks.title: The Jewish War
keyWorks.about: the rising against Rome, in which he commanded in Galilee

keyWorks.title: Jewish Antiquities
keyWorks.about: the history of his people in twenty books, with the two passages that name Jesus

keyWorks.title: Life
keyWorks.about: his own account of himself, written to answer his accusers

remembered: Origen, more than a century later, cites Josephus on James the brother of Jesus, and says Josephus did not accept Jesus as Christ.
Eusebius of Caesarea quotes the longer passage on Jesus in his Church History.
Jerome, late in the fourth century, gives the passage on Jesus in Latin in his notice of Josephus, and in his Latin Jesus was believed to be the Christ.
Sozomen, a church historian of the fifth century, writes that in these lines Josephus all but proclaims that Christ, by comparison of works, is God.

Michael the Syrian, a Syriac Orthodox patriarch of the twelfth century, gives the passage in his chronicle, in Jean-Baptiste Chabot's French, with the words that it is thought Jesus was the Messiah, but not on the witness of the chiefs of the people.

uncertain: Origen says Josephus did not accept Jesus as Christ, which sits badly with the line "He was the Christ."
Origen also cites Josephus as saying the city fell because of what was done to James. That line is not in the Antiquities as we have it.
Josephus's prediction that Vespasian would rule is told by Josephus himself and also by the Roman writer Suetonius.

Why Josephus went to Galilee. His Life says the leading men of Jerusalem sent him and two other priests to persuade the rebels to lay down their arms and wait to see what the Romans would do. His War names him general of both Galilees. Both accounts are his own.

How the old copies word the key clause of the passage on Jesus. Eusebius and the Greek copies read that he was the Christ; Jerome's Latin, that he was believed to be the Christ; Michael the Syrian's chronicle, that it is thought he was the Messiah, but not on the witness of the chiefs of the people. Origen, who read the Antiquities, says Josephus did not accept Jesus as the Christ, and in the works held here quotes nothing of a passage on Jesus.

Jerome's notice also says Josephus openly acknowledges that Christ was slain by the Pharisees on account of the greatness of his miracles, that John the Baptist was truly a prophet, and that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the murder of James the apostle. None of the three is in the Antiquities as held here.

briefReferences: Jewish War, Book 3, in William Whiston's English: the fall of Jotapata in 67, the cave and the forty men, Vespasian's promise, the secret prayer, and the lots.
Life, in Whiston's English: the emperors' favor at Rome, and his closing words, "let others judge of my character."

Jewish Antiquities, in Whiston's English: finished in the thirteenth year of Domitian, about 93. Book 18: Herod kills John the Baptist, "a good man", fearing his hold on the people; and the passage on Jesus. Book 20: the chief priest has James, "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ", stoned.
Origen, Against Celsus 1.47, and Commentary on Matthew 10.17, in Greek with the Ante-Nicene English: Josephus on John and on James, and that he did not accept Jesus as the Christ.
Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History 1.9 and 1.11, in Arthur McGiffert's English: the passage on Jesus, quoted against the forged Acts of Pilate as the word of a Hebrew historian.
Jerome, Illustrious Men 13, in Latin: Jesus was believed to be the Christ.

Jewish War, Book 3, in Whiston's English: the men's offer of a sword, to die as general of the Jewish people or as a traitor to them, and their rush at him calling him a coward (lines 110897-110901, 111066-111069); the lots, and Josephus left last with one other man (lines 111107-111133).

Jewish War, opening, and Jewish Antiquities, opening, in Whiston's English: why he wrote, because others had written falsely of the war, out of flattery to the Romans or hatred of the Jewish people (lines 91740-91751), and to set his people's history before the Greeks (lines 5546-5551).
Life, in Whiston's English: his defense against Justus, a rival historian who, he says, had written falsely of him (lines 4614-4632).

Jewish Antiquities, in Whiston's English: Book 18, John, a good man who urged righteousness toward one another and piety toward God, and Herod's fear of a rising (lines 82087-82123); Book 18, the passage on Jesus, between a riot under Pilate and another disaster (lines 81390-81424); Book 20, the council of judges, the charge of breaking the law and the protest of the fairest-minded citizens (lines 91000-91047).

Eusebius of Caesarea, Church History 1.11 and 2.23, in Arthur McGiffert's English: the lines on John and Jesus (lines 9145-9164, 9228-9246) and the lines on James (lines 13566-13614); Church History 9.5: the forged records sent out with the emperor's approval (lines 47945-47951).

The passage on Jesus in Greek, as the Greek Illustrious Men and the Greek Martyrdom of Donatus quote it (lines 50993-51005 of the Jerome file; lines 80255-80262 of the Acta Sanctorum file): the wording the modern English of the quotation follows.
The phrase on James in Greek: Origen, Commentary on Matthew 10.17 (lines 3729-3730), and Eusebius's quotation in McGiffert's note (lines 13596-13602).

quotationOriginals.modern: I give them my hands willingly, and I am content to live. And I declare openly that I do not go over to the Romans as a deserter from the Jewish people, but as a servant sent by you.
quotationOriginals.printed: I willingly give them my hands, and am content to live. And I protest openly, that I do not go over to the Romans as a deserter of the Jews, but as a minister from thee.
quotationOriginals.work: Josephus, Jewish War 3.8, tr. William Whiston
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The Greek is not held. The modern English is made from Whiston's English alone, and gives his "minister" as "servant sent by you".

quotationOriginals.modern: About this time there lived Jesus, a wise man, if one ought to call him a man. For he did astonishing deeds, and taught people who gladly receive the truth. He won over many of the Jewish people, and many of the Greeks as well. This man was the Christ.
quotationOriginals.printed: And there lived at that time Jesus, a wise man, if indeed it be proper to call him a man. For he was a doer of wonderful works, and a teacher of such men as receive the truth in gladness. And he attached to himself many of the Jews, and many also of the Greeks. He was the Christ.
quotationOriginals.work: Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.3, as Eusebius quotes it in Church History 1.11, tr. Arthur McGiffert
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The modern English follows the Greek of the passage as two later Christian books quote it, the Greek Illustrious Men printed with Jerome's Latin (lines 50993-51005 of that file) and the Greek Martyrdom of Donatus, Macarius and Theodore (lines 80255-80262). Both scans are damaged and agree on these sentences. The clause Ὁ Χριστὸς οὗτος ἦν, this man was the Christ, stands clean at line 80262 of the Acta Sanctorum file and lines 50948-50949 of the Jerome file. Whiston's English (lines 81405-81411 of the Josephus file) reads "Gentiles" where McGiffert's reads "Greeks", and "He was [the] Christ".

Whiston's English reads "whose name was James"; McGiffert's English reads "James by name" (line 13593).

shortDescription: Josephus was a Jewish priest from Jerusalem who commanded in Galilee when the Jewish people rose against Rome, gave himself up to the Roman general Vespasian in 67, and wrote his people's history at Rome. A few lines in it tell of John the Baptist, of James the brother of Jesus, and of Jesus, and Christians copied them for centuries.

lines.text: Born to Matthias in the first year of the reign of Gaius.
lines.note: The year follows the date of Gaius's accession.

lines.text: Born into a family descended from priests, of the first of the twenty-four courses of priests, and on his mother's side of the family of the Hasmonean kings and high priests.
lines.note: His own account.

lines.text: The high priests and leading men of the city come to ask his opinion on points of the law.
lines.note: His own account of himself.

lines.text: Tries the three Jewish schools, the Pharisees, the Sadducees and the Essenes, then spends three years with a desert ascetic named Banus.
Returns to the city and begins to follow the rule of the Pharisees.

timeline.headline: The rising against Rome, and Galilee
timeline.witness: Josephus, in two books that differ

lines.text: The Jewish people's war with Rome begins; Josephus says they were forced into it by necessity.
lines.note: His own view of why.

lines.when: After the Roman governor Gessius is beaten
lines.text: The leading men of Jerusalem send Josephus and two other priests to Galilee, to persuade the rebels there to lay down their arms and wait to see what the Romans would do.
lines.note: In his War he is named general of both Galilees, with the city of Gamala under his command (lines 106926-106929). The two books differ on why he went.

timeline.headline: Jotapata, the cave and the lots

lines.text: Jotapata, a walled town in Galilee, falls in the thirteenth year of Nero. Josephus counts 1,200 captives and 40,000 dead.
lines.note: The counts are his own.

lines.text: The Romans hunt him. He leaps into a deep pit with a hidden den beside it, where forty men of standing are already hiding.
The Romans take a woman who had been hiding with them, and he is found.
Vespasian sends two officers to promise him his life. He fears a trap until a third, Nicanor, an old acquaintance of his, comes.
He remembers dreams in which, he says, God had shown him the coming calamities of the Jewish people and the fate of the Roman emperors.
lines.note: His own claim, told in his voice.

lines.text: He prays in secret, telling God he gives himself up willingly and goes over to the Romans as God's servant, not as a deserter from the Jewish people.
The men with him offer him a sword: he can die as general of the Jewish people or as a traitor to them. They rush at him with their swords and call him a coward.
He proposes that they draw lots, each to be killed in turn by the next. He is left last with one other man, by chance or by God's providence, he says, and persuades him to live.
lines.note: His own telling; no other account is held.

lines.text: Brought before Vespasian, he tells him that he will be emperor, and his son with him. Vespasian thinks it a trick to save his life.
lines.reference: Josephus, Jewish War, lines 111175-111200; Suetonius, Vespasian 5
lines.note: Suetonius, a Roman writer, also records that Josephus, in chains, declared that Vespasian would free him and would then be emperor.

timeline.headline: Freed by Vespasian, and the siege of Jerusalem

lines.text: Vespasian, made emperor, remembers the prediction and is troubled that Josephus is still in chains. At Titus's urging the chain is cut through.
At the siege of Jerusalem, Titus sends him to speak to the defenders in their own language. He goes round the wall and begs them to spare themselves, their country and their Temple.
He says he is often in danger of death: the Jewish people want him punished, and the Romans, whenever they are beaten, blame his treachery and ask the emperors to punish him as a traitor.
lines.note: His own account; both sides call him a traitor.

lines.text: Titus lets him take what he wishes from the ruins. He asks for his family's liberty and the holy books, then the life of his brother and fifty friends, and has about 190 captive women and children he knew set free. He finds three friends crucified and tells Titus, who has them taken down; two die and one recovers.

timeline.headline: Rome and the books
timeline.witness: Josephus, in the Life, the War and the Antiquities

lines.text: At Rome, Vespasian gives him an apartment in his old house, Roman citizenship and a yearly pension. Titus keeps the same respect for him, and Domitian punishes his Jewish accusers and frees his land in Judea from tax.
lines.note: His own account.

lines.text: He translates into Greek his history of the war, first written in the language of his country, because others, he says, gave false accounts out of flattery to the Romans or hatred of the Jewish people.
The war history opens with Joseph, son of Matthias, a Hebrew by birth and a priest, who at first fought against the Romans himself.
He finishes the Jewish Antiquities, his people's history in twenty books, in the thirteenth year of Domitian and the fifty-sixth of his own life. He says he wrote it for the Greeks.
In the Life he answers Justus, a rival historian who, he says, wrote falsely of him.
The Life ends: this is the account of the actions of his whole life, and others may judge his character by it as they please.
Some Jewish people take the destruction of Herod's army as God's punishment for Herod's killing of John, called the Baptist.
lines.note: Herod's war with the Arab king Aretas, whose daughter Herod had married, comes first in the same book (lines 82009-82065).

lines.text: Josephus calls John a good man who told the Jewish people to practice righteousness toward one another and piety toward God, and to come to baptism, a washing for the cleansing of the body, the soul already made clean by right living.
Herod fears that John's hold on the people may lead to a rising, and has him sent a prisoner to Macherus and put to death.

Between a riot under Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea, and another disaster, a passage of about a hundred words on Jesus: a wise man and a doer of wonderful works, who drew over many Jewish people and many of the Gentiles, and who was the Christ, the Messiah, the anointed one the Jewish people awaited. It says Pilate, at the suggestion of the leading men, condemned him to the cross, that he appeared alive to those who loved him on the third day, and that the Christians, named after him, are not extinct.
lines.note: How much of this passage Josephus wrote is contested. Its wonder is told in the passage's own voice.

lines.text: The younger Ananus, the high priest and a Sadducee, one of a school Josephus says judged offenders harshly, calls a council of judges while Festus is dead and Albinus is still on the road. He brings before it the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others, charges them with breaking the law, and has them stoned.

The fairest-minded citizens dislike what was done. They ask King Agrippa to tell Ananus to act so no more, and tell Albinus on his way that Ananus had no right to call a council without his consent. Albinus writes to Ananus in anger, and Agrippa takes the high priesthood from him after three months.

timeline.headline: Origen on John, James and Jesus
timeline.witness: Origen, in the Ante-Nicene English and the Greek

lines.text: In Against Celsus, written when he was over sixty, Origen says Josephus bears witness to John as a Baptist, who promised purification to those who underwent the rite.
lines.reference: Origen, Against Celsus 1.47, lines 37930-37941; Eusebius, Church History 6.36, lines 37090-37107

lines.text: He says that Josephus, although not believing in Jesus as the Christ, said the disasters of Jerusalem came to the Jewish people as a punishment for the death of James the Just, the brother of Jesus called Christ.
lines.note: The Antiquities as held here has no such line.

lines.text: In his Commentary on Matthew he says the same of James, and adds that it is wonderful that Josephus, though he did not accept Jesus as Christ, still gave testimony that the righteousness of James was so great.
lines.reference: Origen, Commentary on Matthew 10.17, Ante-Nicene English lines 30620-30629, Greek lines 3729-3733
lines.note: Origen's Greek reads our Jesus; the Ante-Nicene English leaves out our. In the works held here, Origen quotes nothing of a passage on Jesus.

timeline.headline: Eusebius copies the passages and sets them against forged records
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, in McGiffert's English

lines.text: In Church History 1.11 he copies the lines on John and the passage on Jesus.
lines.note: In his copy the key clause reads that he was the Christ.

lines.text: He sets these words of an historian who was himself a Hebrew against forged records of Pilate's dealings with Jesus.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History 1.9 and 1.11, lines 8924-8932 and 9242-9246

lines.text: He says the forgers wrote Acts of Pilate and our Savior full of every kind of blasphemy against Christ, sent them with the emperor's approval to the whole of the empire, and ordered that schoolmasters give them to their scholars to learn by heart.
lines.note: The forgers' own text is lost; only Eusebius's account of it is held.

lines.text: In Church History 2.23 he gives Josephus's account of James's stoning, and cites Josephus as saying that these things happened to the Jewish people to avenge James the Just.
lines.note: The avenging line is not in the Antiquities as held here.

lines.text: In Church History 3.5 he reads the fall of Jerusalem as God's judgment on those who committed such outrages against Christ and his apostles, and sends readers who want the details to Josephus's history.
lines.note: Eusebius's own reading.

lines.text: He says Josephus was honored with a statue at Rome, and his works were judged worthy of a place in the library.
lines.note: Jerome repeats it; no earlier source is held.

timeline.headline: Jerome gives the passage in Latin

lines.text: In his notice of Josephus, Jerome gives the passage on Jesus in Latin, and in his Latin Jesus was believed to be the Christ.
lines.reference: Jerome, Illustrious Men 13, Latin lines 50905-50907, English lines 39728-39729
lines.note: Eusebius's copy reads that he was the Christ.

lines.text: The notice also says Josephus openly acknowledges that Christ was slain by the Pharisees on account of the greatness of his miracles, that John the Baptist was truly a prophet, and that Jerusalem was destroyed because of the murder of James the apostle.
lines.reference: Jerome, Illustrious Men 13, English lines 39720-39724, Latin lines 50852-50857
lines.note: None of these three is in the Antiquities as held here.

lines.text: Sozomen, a church historian, calls Josephus a noteworthy witness to the truth concerning Christ, and writes that in these words he all but proclaims that Christ, by comparison of works, is God.
lines.note: Sozomen's own reading.

lines.text: In the Greek Martyrdom of Donatus, Macarius tells the emperor Diocletian that Josephus, a priest from Jerusalem, bears witness that Christ was true God, and quotes the passage.
lines.reference: Martyrdom of Donatus, Macarius and Theodore, Greek lines 80250-80284, Latin lines 80364-80367
lines.note: A martyr's legend; the speech is the legend's own, and it gives no date.

lines.text: Michael the Syrian, a Syriac Orthodox patriarch, gives the passage in his chronicle: it is thought that Jesus was the Messiah, but not on the witness of the chiefs of the people.
lines.reference: Michael the Syrian, Chronicle, in Chabot's French, lines 11161-11165 and 11230-11236
lines.note: The Syriac is not held here; this is a French translation.
